cards.text: This is a psalm of David, for the choirmaster, for Jeduthun, one of the men chosen to give thanks to the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:41). David opens by telling us about a promise he made himself. The wicked are around, and he's decided to be VERY careful about one thing.

cards.question: With the wicked around, David decides to guard his ___ so he won't sin.

cards.text: He says, “I will guard my mouth with a muzzle as long as the wicked are present.” Most of us just bite our tongue, friend, but David went out and got a MUZZLE.

cards.question: True or false: While David keeps that muzzle on, he still lets himself say good things.

cards.text: So David stays speechless and still, not even saying good things. And his sorrow? It gets stirred up.

cards.question: David keeps thinking it over, holding it all in. What does he say his heart does?

cards.text: As he mulls it over, the fire burns, like an oven with the door shut and NOBODY watching the timer. Then David finally speaks, and he speaks to the LORD.

cards.question: After all that silence, what's the first thing David asks the LORD to show him?

answers.text: His end and the measure of his days
The plans the wicked have against him
The reason his sorrow got stirred up

cards.text: Then David pulls out the measuring tape, friend. He says the LORD has made his days as handbreadths.

cards.question: David says the LORD has made his days as handbreadths. What is he saying about his life?

cards.text: He says his lifetime is as nothing before the LORD, and “Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath.” AT HIS BEST, friend, and he's still gone faster than a fresh batch on the cooling rack when my kids were around.

cards.question: David says every man goes about like a phantom and bustles in vain. He heaps up riches, but what doesn't he know?

answers.text: How much he has saved up

cards.question: David asks, “And now, O Lord, for what do I wait?” True or false: He says his hope is in the riches a man heaps up.

cards.text: His hope is in the LORD, and he asks the LORD to deliver him from all his transgressions and not make him the reproach of fools. I get it, baker, NOBODY wants to be the joke in the group chat.

cards.question: David goes mute again. This time he won't open his mouth because of what the ___ did.

cards.text: Then David asks the LORD to remove His scourge from him, and says he's perishing by the force of His hand. Friend, I think this man is running on his last crumb.

cards.question: David says the LORD disciplines and corrects a man for his iniquity, and each man is but a vapor. True or false: What that man holds dear stays safe.
David begs the LORD to hear his prayer and not be deaf to his weeping. How does he describe himself?

answers.text: A foreigner dwelling with the LORD
A servant guarding the LORD's house
A soldier fighting for the LORD

cards.text: A stranger, he says, like all his fathers before him. Now lean in, friend, because David's last line is not the ending you'd expect.

cards.question: In David's last line, he wants to be cheered again before he departs and is no more. What does he ask the LORD to do?

answers.text: Turn His gaze away from him

rule.text: He calls the baker "baker" or "friend," and talks to one baker at a time. Never "my baker," "kids" or "sweetie."

findings.problem: The card says David 'made himself' a 'promise.' Psalm 39:1 only says 'I said, I will…'. The text doesn't say who he said it to, and it doesn't call it a promise. Something like 'David opens by telling us what he decided' keeps to the text.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'It is full of trouble' can be argued as true of David's life elsewhere in the passage. He has stirred sorrow (39:2), the LORD's scourge, and 'I am perishing' (39:10). A baker could argue it's right. Replace it with something false everywhere in the psalm.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: The joke has his kids eating a fresh batch off the cooling rack. His kids are cookie cutters, and in the backstory it's the Miller family who steal dough. Cutters eating cookies adds something new to his world, and a baker who knows the kids would say 'huh?'. Keep the image of a batch vanishing fast, but drop the kids eating it.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: 'He heaps up riches, but what doesn't he know?' asks the baker to finish the line 'he heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away' (39:6). The baker can't reason their way to that wording. Ask about the meaning instead, for example what David is saying about all that bustling and heaping up.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: 'David goes mute again. This time…' treats 39:9 as a second silence, separate from 39:2. The text only says 'I have become mute' and doesn't say how it connects to the earlier silence. Tell 39:9 without 'again' and 'this time.'

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: No story card sets this one up, and nothing earlier points toward 'foreigner' over 'servant' or 'soldier.' It's a pure discovery pick. Cards 8, 12, 15 and 20 are also close to discovery, so almost half the choice cards can't be reasoned out. Add a setup line, for example tying it back to how short life is, or ask a different question.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: 'David's last line is not the ending you'd expect' sets up card 20 by ruling out its ordinary wrong answers ('Give him a long life,' 'Bring his enemies down'). It tells the baker to pick the odd one out. Use a neutral lead-in to the last line.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.
